page: Google Cloud Platform n2-standard-8 is a general-purpose virtual machine instance configured with 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of system memory. Powered by an Intel Xeon processor operating at a base frequency of 2.8 GHz, this x86_64 architecture server features 4 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled, yielding 2 threads per core. The CPU allocation is dedicated, supported by a cache hierarchy consisting of a 32 KB L1 data cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and 33 MB L3 cache. It includes hardware flags such as AVX, AVX512F, AVX512_VNNI, and AES cryptography support. This instance does not include bundled local storage or integrated GPUs.

Benchmark evaluations place the n2-standard-8 primarily in the average performance tier for multi-core processing, memory bandwidth, and standard database operations. Specifically, the instance achieves average ratings in stress-ng multi-core CPU performance, Geekbench multi-core scores, and Passmark database operations. Redis SET operations reach 7.12 million operations per second, and static web serving throughput is measured at 6.9 GB/sec. However, performance tradeoffs are evident in single-core tasks and specialized workloads. The stress-ng single-core CPU performance, bzip3 multi-threaded decompression, and Geekbench ray tracing and image processing benchmarks fall into the bottom 25% tier. Additionally, prompt processing for small language models is weak, although text generation speeds remain average.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the n2-standard-8 offers a balanced resource density of 4.0 GB of RAM per vCPU, aligning with standard general-purpose profiles. This balance makes it suitable for workloads that require steady, dedicated CPU resources without the premium cost of memory-optimized or GPU-accelerated hardware. Recommended workloads include general software compilation, text processing, static web serving, and standard database operations. It is less suitable for compute-intensive physics simulations, real-time image processing, or heavy single-threaded tasks due to its lower single-core performance profile.
